h1:
Sa Kaeo Khmer Temple Trail
Sdok Kok Thom–Khao Noi Si Chomphu
intro: Say "Khmer temple" and most people jump straight to Buriram or Surin. But Sa Kaeo is an overlooked gateway to Khmer history out east. Here you'll find Sdok Kok Thom, a stone temple whose inscription traces the Khmer royal line across more than a century, and Khao Noi Si Chomphu, home to the oldest dated inscription found in Thailand. We've mapped out a route you can drive at an easy pace, stop by stop, with opening hours and the things worth checking before you actually go.

blocks.html: Sa Kaeo sits at Thailand's far eastern edge, right against the Cambodian border, and it was a Khmer corridor long before the Angkor period. What's left are stone temples scattered across Khok Sung, Aranyaprathet and Ta Phraya districts. The upside is that crowds are still thin — you can wander quietly without fighting anyone for a photo angle. The trade-off is that facilities are thin too, so pack water, a hat and a full tank of fuel before you set off.

blocks.text: Which temples are on this trail

blocks.html: The Sa Kaeo Khmer temple trail comes down to three sites that are realistic to visit and still have something to see. We've ordered them by significance and how easy they are to reach.

items.name: Sdok Kok Thom (Khok Sung district)
items.blurb: A sandstone-and-laterite temple facing east, with a central sanctuary, two libraries, and a gallery and outer wall around it. The standout is the Sdok Kok Thom inscription, which records the Khmer royal line continuously for over 200 years, going back to the reign of Jayavarman II. It's now a historical park under the Fine Arts Department, with an information centre to walk through before you reach the temple itself.

items.name: Khao Noi Si Chomphu (Aranyaprathet district)
items.blurb: A brick temple on a low hill about 80 metres high. There were originally three towers; what remains is the central prang plus two earthen mounds. This is where the Khao Noi inscription was found, dated to 559 of the Mahasakaraj era — equivalent to 637 CE — making it the oldest dated inscription in Thailand. You can climb the 254-step staircase, or drive around via the temple and walk a little further. The top is a viewpoint where you can also camp and catch the sun.

items.name: Khao Lon (Ta Phraya district)
items.blurb: A brick shrine on a sandstone hilltop, dating to around the 11th century CE, with brickwork laid so tightly the joints sit flush — classic ancient Khmer craftsmanship. It's fairly far out and isolated, best suited to people who really want to complete the temple set. Check the route and the border situation ahead of time before you go.
items.meta: Deep inside Ta Phraya · Access road is remote

blocks.text: Sdok Kok Thom — the stop not to rush

blocks.html: Sdok Kok Thom literally means "the great temple overgrown with reeds." It stands at Ban Nong Ya Kaeo, Khok Sung subdistrict, Khok Sung district. What makes it more important than a typical stone temple is the inscription — it reads like a logbook of the Khmer royal line, listing kings and events across several generations. Before you walk in, stop at the information centre first; you'll actually understand what you're looking at, rather than just passing a pile of stones.

items: Orientation and light — the temple faces east, so morning light pours into the gateways nicely and gives the carved stone real depth in photos.
Easy walking — the ground is fairly flat and you can loop around without much effort, but there's little shade, so go before the sun gets harsh.
Food nearby — there are few shops around the temple, so top up on water and snacks in Khok Sung or Aranyaprathet town first.

blocks.title: Check before you make the drive
blocks.html: The information centre and the park itself have closed for renovation at times and adjusted their hours now and then. Before driving all that way, check the Sdok Kok Thom Historical Park page or call the Fine Arts Department first, so you don't waste the trip.

blocks.text: Khao Noi Si Chomphu — climbing up to Thailand's oldest inscription

blocks.html: Khao Noi Si Chomphu is in Khlong Nam Sai subdistrict, Aranyaprathet district, about 12 kilometres from town. The temple is a mortarless brick structure, thought to have been built around the 7th century CE and restored in the 10th. What gets historians excited is a lintel in the Khmer Sambor Prei Kuk style, plus the Khao Noi inscription clearly dated to 637 CE — making this a key marker for studying the early Khmer civilization in Thailand.

There are two ways up. The first is the 254-step staircase — tiring but not brutal; take it in stages and rest along the way. The other is to drive toward Wat Khao Noi for about another kilometre and then walk roughly 250 metres on foot, which works better if you're with mixed ages or bringing older relatives along. The top is a wide viewpoint, and some people camp overnight to catch sunrise and sunset.

blocks.title: Morning or evening beats midday
blocks.html: The stairs and the temple terrace have almost no shade, so going around noon means heat and harsh light. Aim for early when it opens or late afternoon near sunset — both an easier climb and nicer light.

Coming from Bangkok, it's about a 3–4 hour drive to Sa Kaeo. Staying one night around Aranyaprathet means you don't have to rush and can see every temple. Here's a route we've put together to keep things flowing.

items.activity: Leave Bangkok heading for Sa Kaeo
items.note: Fill up on fuel and food before reaching the district — convenience stores get sparser toward the end of the route.

items.activity: Arrive in Khok Sung, find lunch in town
items.note: Made-to-order shops and local noodle stalls are on hand. Eat up before heading into the temple.

items.activity: Enter Sdok Kok Thom, starting at the info centre before the temple
items.note: Allow about 1.5–2 hours to walk around and take photos. Shade is scarce, so bring a hat and water.
There are hotels and guesthouses in town across a range of prices — book ahead on long weekends.
The town centre has an evening market and local restaurants. Eat well, then rest up for the early climb tomorrow.

items.activity: Breakfast, then head for Khao Noi Si Chomphu
items.note: Going early makes the climb easier while the sun is still gentle.

items.activity: Climb Khao Noi Si Chomphu — the prang, the inscription and the view up top
items.note: Take the 254 steps, or drive around via the temple if you're bringing older relatives.

items.activity: Head down, stop at Rong Kluea Market or pick up souvenirs before leaving
items.note: You can add Khao Lon in Ta Phraya if you have time and have checked the route.

items.activity: Lunch in Aranyaprathet, then start the drive home
items.note: Allow for evening traffic if you're heading back on a Sunday.

blocks.text: What to know about the border before you go

blocks.html: Several temples on this trail sit close to the Thailand–Cambodia border, especially around Ta Phraya and some outlying areas. The border situation can shift from time to time, and there are occasionally closures or restricted access. If you're set on the deeper sites or anything near the boundary line, always check the news and ask local authorities first. And if you're thinking of crossing over to Poipet, have your passport and documents ready and confirm the checkpoint is operating normally on the day you go.

items: Check the situation first — especially sites near the border line such as Khao Lon and Ta Phraya. Don't rely on old information.
Prepare your documents — if you're crossing at the Khlong Luek–Poipet checkpoint, you'll need a passport and should check the latest entry and exit conditions.
Signal and fuel — phone signal is weak in places, so save offline maps and fill the tank before heading into remote areas.

blocks.text: Getting the most out of Sa Kaeo's Khmer temples

items.name: Self-driving is by far the easiest
items.blurb: The temples are spread across different districts and public transport doesn't reach them. Having your own car or a rental lets you collect them all in a single day.

items.name: Dress for walking
items.blurb: Non-slip trainers, a hat, sunglasses and water on hand — several sites mean walking in full sun and climbing stairs.

items.name: Read the signs before you shoot
items.blurb: These temples have a lot of backstory. Read the signs or hear it at the info centre first and you'll notice the lintel details and inscriptions you'd usually walk right past.

faq.q: How many Khmer temples can you visit in Sa Kaeo?
faq.a: There are three main sites that are realistic to visit and still have something to see: Sdok Kok Thom in Khok Sung district, Khao Noi Si Chomphu in Aranyaprathet district, and Khao Lon in Ta Phraya district. The first two are easy to reach and work well in one trip, while Khao Lon is further out and you should check the route first.

faq.q: What time does Sdok Kok Thom open, and is there an entry fee?
faq.a: It's generally open daily around 08.30–16.30 with no entry fee, but the park and info centre have closed for renovation at times and adjusted their hours now and then. Before you go, it's worth checking the Sdok Kok Thom Historical Park page or the Fine Arts Department again.

faq.q: Do you have to climb all the stairs at Khao Noi Si Chomphu?
faq.a: Not necessarily. There's a 254-step staircase for those who want to walk, but you can also drive around via Wat Khao Noi for about another kilometre and then walk roughly 250 metres on foot — handy if you're bringing older relatives or kids.

faq.q: Why is Khao Noi Si Chomphu historically important?
faq.a: Because the Khao Noi inscription found here is clearly dated to 637 CE, making it the oldest dated inscription in Thailand. A lintel in the Khmer Sambor Prei Kuk style was also found, making the site key evidence of the early Khmer civilization on Thai soil.

faq.q: Where should you stay overnight when visiting Sa Kaeo's Khmer temples?
faq.a: Most people stay in Aranyaprathet town, which has hotels and guesthouses across a range of prices. It sits midway between the sites and close to Rong Kluea Market and the border checkpoint, making a relaxed two-day trip easy to plan.
